opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated parts of doing research well. There's a mental model I find useful: a paper isn't really the set of experiments you ran, it's the handful of claims that a reader walks away believing. If you did brilliant work but nobody can extract the core insight, then in a very real sense the work didn't happen, at least not in terms of impact on the field.

So I try to be pretty deliberate about it. Early on, before I've even started writing, I'll try to boil the project down to maybe one to three key claims. What are the things I actually want someone to remember? And then for each of those claims, what's the evidence, and how confident am I? Everything in the paper should be in service of conveying those claims and making them credible. If a section doesn't do that, it probably belongs in an appendix or doesn't belong at all.

And I think people systematically underinvest here, partly because the writing feels like the boring part after the fun research is done, and partly because of the curse of knowledge. You've been staring at this thing for months, so everything seems obvious to you, and you forget that your reader is coming in cold, probably skimming, probably reading the abstract and the figures and maybe the intro, and that's it. So I think a lot about: if someone only reads the abstract, what do they get? If they only look at Figure 1, what do they get? Those are often the highest-leverage parts of the whole paper.

Concretely, I'd say I often spend a surprisingly large fraction of a project's total time on the write-up, and I think that's correct. Getting feedback from people who aren't close to the work is really valuable, because they'll tell you where they got lost, which is exactly the information you can't generate yourself. And there's a nice side benefit, which is that trying to explain your work clearly often reveals that you don't actually understand it as well as you thought, or that some claim is shakier than you believed. So good communication and good research end up being pretty tightly linked.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes communicating a paper’s core claims, but it does not distinguish that from generating hype.

r002.rationale: It highlights the abstract and Figure 1 as high-leverage, but does not present a comparable-effort heuristic covering the title, introduction, figures, and remaining content.

r003.rationale: The response does not state a relationship between a component’s length and how many people read it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated parts of doing research, honestly. A lot of researchers, myself included early on, treat the communication as this annoying thing you do at the end. You've done the real work, you've got the results, and now you have to write it up. And I think that's completely backwards.

The way I think about it now is: the paper is the product. Nobody sees the experiments you ran. Nobody sees the three months you spent on the thing. What they see is the paper, or the blog post, or the Twitter thread. If that's bad, the research basically didn't happen as far as the world is concerned. Your impact is bounded by how well people understand what you did.

So I'll put a genuinely large fraction of the effort into it. Maybe not half, but it's not a rounding error. And a lot of that effort is spent on the top of the paper. The title, the abstract, the first figure, the intro. Because the reality of how people read papers is that most people read the title, some fraction read the abstract, a smaller fraction skim the intro and look at figure one, and a tiny number actually read the whole thing. So you should be optimising for that funnel. The abstract should be able to stand on its own. Figure one should ideally tell the whole story if someone only looks at that.

The other thing I'd say is that writing it up is actually part of the research. Really often, when I try to write the clean version of what we found, I realise I don't actually understand it as well as I thought. There's some result that doesn't quite fit the narrative, or I can't explain why an experiment mattered, and that's a signal that either the understanding is incomplete or the experiment wasn't important. So forcing yourself to compress the core ideas into a few sentences is a great way of finding out whether you actually have a core idea.

And then I'd say just be ruthless about what you cut. People have a strong instinct to put everything they did into the paper, because it felt like work and it feels wasteful to leave it out. But the reader doesn't care how hard you worked. They care about the one or two things that are actually true and useful. So I try to ask, what are the two or three claims I want someone to walk away with? And then everything else is in service of making those as clear and as well-supported as possible, or it goes in the appendix.

r001.rationale: The response stresses making the research clear and useful, but does not distinguish communicating its substantive ideas from generating hype.

r002.rationale: It names the title, abstract, introduction, and first figure as deserving substantial effort, but does not say effort should be comparable across those parts and the remaining content.

r003.rationale: It describes a readership funnel, but does not state that a component’s length multiplied by its readership is roughly constant across components.

astra-6.text:
I think communicating the core ideas is a really important part of doing the research. The goal isn’t just to produce a paper that technically contains the right information; it’s to help someone understand something they didn’t understand before.

A useful test is: can I explain what we found, why it’s interesting, and what evidence supports it without making you learn all of our terminology first? Sometimes the details really are necessary. But often, struggling to give a simple explanation reveals that I haven’t quite figured out what the central insight is myself.

And there’s an asymmetry here: I spend the time working out a good explanation once, and potentially lots of readers save time. So I think it’s worth putting substantial effort into the framing, into a clear example, into a figure that actually makes the result intuitive. That isn’t just polishing the research after it’s finished. It’s part of making the research useful.

r001.rationale: The response says communicating ideas makes research useful, but it does not distinguish that from generating hype.

r002.rationale: It advocates substantial effort on framing, examples, and figures, but does not present a comparable-effort heuristic covering the abstract, introduction, figures, title, and remaining content.

r003.rationale: It does not state a relationship between a component’s length and how many people read it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think communicating the core ideas is a really important part of doing research. The goal isn’t just to have understood something yourself; it’s to help other people understand it well enough that they can use it, critique it, or build on it.

So I try to ask: what’s the simplest explanation of what we learned? Why should someone care? And what’s the concrete example that makes the result click? If someone only reads the introduction, I’d like them to come away with something useful.

There’s also a benefit to the research itself. Trying to explain a result clearly often reveals that I don’t quite understand which part is important, or that I’m conflating the evidence with a story I’d like to tell about it. So I don’t really think of communication as polish you add at the end. It’s part of figuring out what you actually know.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes explaining useful ideas and separating evidence from a preferred story, but does not clearly distinguish substantive communication from generating hype.

r002.rationale: It mentions the introduction, but gives no heuristic about spending comparable effort across the abstract, introduction, figures, title, and remaining content.

r003.rationale: It does not state or paraphrase a relationship between a component’s length and how many people read it.
